title: Gas Motions in Hydra-A: XRISM Constraints on ICM Kinematics Across Jet-Inflated Cavities
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures; Submitted to ApJ. Comments are welcome at this stage
summary: We report on two deep XRISM observations of the central and northern regions of Hydra-A's X-ray atmosphere covering the bubbles inflated by jets from the central galaxy's active galactic nucleus (AGN). We use spatial-spectral mixing that combines Chandra's high spatial resolution with XRISM's high spectral resolution to investigate atmospheric kinematics. The atmospheric velocity dispersion in the northern region, $σ_v = 140^{+30}_{-20}$ km s$^{-1}$, is comparable to that in the central region ($σ_v = 162 \pm 10$ km s$^{-1}$). We show that the motion of the large-scale cocoon shock front could be responsible for the large dispersion toward the north. The velocity dispersion in the northeast quarter of the central pointing, $σ_v = 260 \pm 50$ km s$^{-1}$, is among the highest dispersions measured. This region contains an X-ray-bright feature previously identified as metal-rich, possibly consisting of gas uplifted in the wake of previous-generation cavities. The dispersions in all other quarter regions are low ($σ_v \leq 120$ km s$^{-1}$) and consistent with previous XRISM results from other objects. The kinetic energy at the center is comparable to the enthalpies of the cavities, while in the north, it is roughly an order of magnitude smaller. The jet thus drives gas motion efficiently at smaller scales ($r < 95$ kpc) and inefficiently at larger scales ($95-317$ kpc toward the north along the jet). A bulk flow toward our line of sight of $-100 \pm 30$ km s$^{-1}$ in the southwest quarter of the central pointing is also observed, possibly due to sloshing.

AI.tldr: XRISM and Chandra observations of Hydra-A reveal atmospheric kinematics in the central and northern regions, with velocity dispersions of ~140-162 km/s, showing efficient jet-driven gas motion at small scales (<95 kpc) but inefficient at larger scales (95-317 kpc), and evidence of a bulk flow (-100 km/s) in the southwest due to sloshing.
AI.motivation: To understand how AGN jets drive gas motion in the intracluster medium (ICM) of galaxy clusters, particularly the efficiency of kinetic energy injection at different spatial scales in Hydra-A's X-ray atmosphere.
AI.method: Spatial-spectral mixing combining Chandra's high spatial resolution with XRISM's high spectral resolution to measure atmospheric velocity dispersions and bulk motions across different regions of Hydra-A's X-ray atmosphere.
AI.result: Northern region velocity dispersion σ_v = 140^{+30}_{-20} km/s; central region σ_v = 162 ± 10 km/s; northeast quarter σ_v = 260 ± 50 km/s (among highest measured); other quarters σ_v ≤ 120 km/s. Kinetic energy at center comparable to cavity enthalpies, but ~10× smaller in the north. Southwest bulk flow of -100 ± 30 km/s detected.
AI.conclusion: Jet-driven gas motion is efficient within ~95 kpc but inefficient beyond, with the cocoon shock front responsible for large northern dispersions. Sloshing may explain the southwest bulk flow.

title: Can We Find the Emission Mechanism Behind the Extremely Bright GRB 230812B?
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, 3 Tables. Submitted to ApJ
summary:
GRB 230812B is a bright long-duration GRB with a luminous, long-lived afterglow and an AstroSat/CZTI polarization measurement during the prompt phase, enabling a joint study of its prompt spectral evolution, polarization, and broadband afterglow. Time-resolved spectroscopy of the prompt emission shows that during the rising phase, the low-energy Band-function index exceeds the synchrotron line of death, favoring the presence of an additional thermal component. At later times, from $T_0+2$ s to $T_0+32$ s, the prompt spectra are consistent with predominantly non-thermal emission. Polarization analysis of the prompt emission in the $300$-$600$ keV band yields a marginal lower limit on the polarization fraction of $Π\gtrsim 50\%$ at the $1σ$ level.
  The long X-ray monitoring of the afterglow shows no jet break over the observed baseline. Multiwavelength afterglow modeling favors a wide jet with an inferred half-opening angle of $θ_j = 15^{+6}_{-4}$ degrees observed close to the jet axis with a viewing angle of $θ_v = 0.9^{+1.8}_{-0.6}$ degrees. The inferred circumburst density is low, $n_0 = 1.2^{+0.3}_{-0.1}\times10^{-4}\,\textrm{cm}^{-3}$, and the isotropic-equivalent kinetic energy of the jet is $E_{{\rm k}, iso} = 4.0^{+1.5}_{-0.8} \times 10^{53}$ erg.
  Taken together, the prompt spectral evolution favors an early phase with a thermal contribution followed by a later phase dominated by non-thermal emission. The polarization constraint in the late prompt phase is consistent with synchrotron emission, although a higher-significance polarization measurement will be required to robustly constrain the magnetic-field geometry and the relative contribution of photospheric emission.

AI.tldr: GRB 230812B is a bright long‑duration gamma‑ray burst with an early thermal component followed by non‑thermal emission; prompt polarization (Π ≳ 50%) is marginally detected, and multiwavelength afterglow modeling yields a wide jet (θj ≈ 15°) viewed nearly on‑axis, with a very low circumburst density (n₀ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ cm⁻³).
AI.motivation: To jointly study the prompt spectral evolution, polarization, and broadband afterglow of GRB 230812B, leveraging a rare simultaneous polarization measurement from AstroSat/CZTI to constrain the emission mechanisms and jet geometry.
AI.method: Time‑resolved spectroscopy of the prompt emission; polarization analysis in the 300–600 keV band; multiwavelength afterglow modeling using forward shocks to infer jet half‑opening angle, viewing angle, circumburst density, and kinetic energy.
AI.result: Early prompt phase shows a thermal component (low‑energy Band index violates the synchrotron line of death); later phases (T₀+2 s to T₀+32 s) are consistent with non‑thermal emission. Polarization fraction Π ≳ 50% at 1σ. No jet break is seen; the inferred jet half‑opening angle is θj = 15⁺⁶₋₄°, viewing angle θv = 0.9⁺¹·⁸₋₀·₆°, low density n₀ = 1.2⁺⁰·³₋₀·₁ × 10⁻⁴ cm⁻³, and Eₖ,ᵢₛₒ = 4.0⁺¹·⁵₋₀·₈ × 10⁵³ erg.
AI.conclusion: The prompt spectral evolution favors an early thermal‑plus‑non‑thermal phase transitioning to later non‑thermal dominance; the polarization marginal detection is consistent with synchrotron emission, but higher significance is needed to constrain the magnetic‑field geometry and photospheric contribution.

title: Time-Domain Axion Searches with Magnetic White Dwarfs
summary: Magnetic white dwarfs can convert photons into axions in their strong magnetic fields, with the conversion probability modulating the light curve as the star rotates. However, this observable is degenerate with intrinsic stellar variability if the background is modeled too simplistically. We develop a controlled background-degeneracy framework that computes the axion-induced modulation from reconstructed stellar magnetic fields while fitting it simultaneously with a flexible Fourier model of the intrinsic light curve. Applying this framework to TESS observations of PG~1015+014 using two independent magnetic field reconstructions, we find that a sinusoidal stellar background can produce an apparent preference for nonzero axion-photon conversion. This preference is absorbed once the background light curve includes the second harmonic, indicating that higher-harmonic stellar variability is a leading degeneracy for precise photometric axion searches in magnetic white dwarfs. Interpreting the two-harmonic fit as a conservative baseline, we obtain competitive constraints for sub-$μ\mathrm{eV}$ axions. We further derive an analytic target-ranking estimate for other TESS magnetic white dwarfs, identifying systems where phase-resolved magnetic modeling would be most valuable for competitive axion probes.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a framework to disentangle axion-induced photometric signals from intrinsic stellar variability in magnetic white dwarfs, showing that higher-harmonic background variability is a key degeneracy and obtaining competitive axion constraints from PG~1015+014.
AI.motivation: Magnetic white dwarfs can convert photons to axions, producing observable modulation in light curves, but this signal is degenerate with intrinsic stellar variability if the background model is oversimplified.
AI.method: A controlled background-degeneracy framework is developed that computes axion-induced modulation from reconstructed magnetic fields while simultaneously fitting a flexible Fourier model of the intrinsic light curve. Applied to TESS observations of PG~1015+014 with two independent magnetic field reconstructions.
AI.result: A sinusoidal background model creates an apparent preference for nonzero axion-photon conversion, but this is absorbed when the second harmonic is included, showing higher-harmonic variability is a leading degeneracy. The two-harmonic fit yields competitive constraints for sub-μeV axions.
AI.conclusion: Higher-harmonic stellar variability must be accounted for in photometric axion searches; the framework provides competitive axion constraints and an analytic target-ranking estimate for other TESS magnetic white dwarfs.

title: Universal scaling between magnetar field and initial spin period for short gamma ray bursts
summary: The $B_p$--$P_0$ correlation serves as a critical probe of magnetar engine physics. Although this scaling relation has been firmly established for long gamma-ray bursts (lGRBs), systematic investigations for short GRBs (sGRBs) remain absent, leaving the physical differences between the two populations poorly constrained. Here we analyze 33 Swift sGRBs exhibiting prominent X-ray plateaus from newborn millisecond magnetar spin-down, and derive their initial spin period $P_0$ and polar magnetic field $B_p$. sGRB magnetars span $P_0 \in [1.73,\,18.28]\ \mathrm{ms}$ and $B_p \in [0.06,\,2.82] \times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{G}$ ($\langle B_p \rangle = 7.05 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{G}$), significantly more magnetized than lGRB magnetars ($B_p \in [0.39,\,23.08] \times 10^{15}\ \mathrm{G}$; $\langle B_p \rangle = 3.69 \times 10^{15}\ \mathrm{G}$). For the first time, we derive consistent power-law $B_p$--$P_0$ correlations for GRBs : the scaling for sGRBs is $\log B_p = (0.84\pm0.07)\log P_0 + (15.79\pm0.07)$, whose slope is highly consistent with that of lGRBs, $\log B_p = (0.83\pm0.09)\log P_0 + (14.92\pm0.06)$. The near-identical slopes imply a universal magnetar spin-down mechanism, while the vertical offset between intercepts traces divergent progenitor channels. This scaling relation thus offers a new diagnostic to disentangle the formation pathways of GRB. Within the framework of the standard spin-up model, the mass accretion rates of sGRBs ($\dot{M} \sim 1 \times 10^{-1}$ to $3 \times 10^{-1}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$) are substantially higher than those of lGRBs ($\dot{M} \sim 10^{-4}$ to $1 \times 10^{-1}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$). Our work completes the missing $B_p$--$P_0$ statistics for sGRBs, quantitatively unifies their magnetar physics with lGRBs, and provides new observational constraints on the origin diversity of relativistic transients.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes the first systematic $B_p$-$P_0$ correlation for short GRB magnetars by analyzing 33 Swift sGRBs with X-ray plateaus. It finds that sGRB magnetars are significantly more magnetized than lGRB magnetars, yet both populations share nearly identical power-law slopes (~0.84), indicating a universal spin-down mechanism, while the vertical offset reveals distinct progenitor channels.
AI.motivation: Although the $B_p$-$P_0$ correlation is well-established for long GRBs, systematic investigations for short GRBs were absent, leaving the physical differences between the two populations poorly constrained.
AI.method: Analyzed 33 Swift sGRBs exhibiting prominent X-ray plateaus from newborn millisecond magnetar spin-down; derived initial spin period $P_0$ and polar magnetic field $B_p$; performed power-law fitting to establish $B_p$-$P_0$ correlations.
AI.result: sGRB magnetars: $P_0 \in [1.73, 18.28]$ ms, $B_p \in [0.06, 2.82] \times 10^{17}$ G (mean $7.05 \times 10^{16}$ G), significantly more magnetized than lGRBs. The $B_p$-$P_0$ slope for sGRBs ($0.84\pm0.07$) is highly consistent with that of lGRBs ($0.83\pm0.09$). Mass accretion rates of sGRBs ($\sim 0.1-0.3\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$) are substantially higher than lGRBs.
AI.conclusion: Completes missing $B_p$-$P_0$ statistics for sGRBs, quantitatively unifies magnetar physics across GRB populations, and provides new observational constraints on the origin diversity of relativistic transients.

title: Star formation powers optical line emission from the CGM
comment: Accept for publication in Science Advances, Figure 1, 2, 3 are the main results
summary: Using integral field spectroscopy, we explore the disk-halo interface, or the inner circumgalactic medium (CGM), of individual galaxies by constructing and analyzing emission-line maps for a large sample (72) of normal, low-redshift galaxies spanning three orders of magnitude in stellar mass and four orders in star formation rate (SFR). We find a steep turnover occurring at $(1-2) R_e$ in the H$α$, [O {\small II}], and [O {\small III}] line emission radial profiles. Beyond this radius, the slope of the line emission radial profiles becomes shallower as the SFR of the central galaxy decreases, which might reflect the strength of the feedback processes. The line emission fluxes at large radius ($(5-10) R_e$ or $\sim (0.1-0.25)r_{\rm vir}$) correlate with the galaxy's SFR, but not with its stellar mass. These findings suggest that ionizing photons escaping from star-forming regions in the central galaxy account for the observed emission line fluxes from the inner CGM, with escape fractions inferred from the [O {\small III}] and [O {\small II}] ratio. Different state-of-the-art theoretical models do not agree on the predicted dependence of cool gas on the SFR of the central galaxies, highlighting the importance of CGM emission line measurements to distinguish between different subgrid models for star formation and feedback processes.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes emission-line maps from 72 low-redshift galaxies to explore the disk-halo interface (inner CGM). They find a steep turnover in line emission at 1-2 R_e, beyond which the slope correlates with SFR. Line emission at large radii (5-10 R_e) correlates with SFR but not stellar mass, suggesting ionizing photons from star-forming regions power the inner CGM emission.
AI.motivation: To understand the disk-halo interface and inner CGM of galaxies by characterizing emission-line properties across a wide range of galaxy stellar masses and star formation rates.
AI.method: Integral field spectroscopy of 72 normal, low-redshift galaxies spanning three orders of magnitude in stellar mass and four orders in SFR, analyzing Hα, [O II], and [O III] emission-line radial profiles.
AI.result: A steep turnover at 1-2 R_e in line emission profiles; beyond that, slope correlates negatively with SFR; large-radius fluxes correlate with SFR but not stellar mass; inferred escape fractions from [O III]/[O II] ratios.
AI.conclusion: Ionizing photons from central star-forming regions likely power the inner CGM emission, and current theoretical models disagree on the cool gas-SFR dependence, emphasizing the need for CGM emission-line measurements to distinguish between feedback models.

title: The XMM-Newton Line Emission Analysis Program (X-LEAP) III: Earth's Magnetospheric X-ray Emission Revealed by 22-Year XMM-Newton Observations
summary: The magnetosphere, protecting the Earth from intense solar activity, is also shaped by the solar wind, while its structure is still uncertain in observation. In this study, we map the X-ray emission in the magnetosphere, which is induced by the charge exchange between the highly-ionized solar wind and the neutral gas around the Earth, known as the magnetospheric solar wind charge exchange (SWCX). In particular, we extract the magnetospheric SWCX in the O VII line emission data adopted from the XMM Line Emission Analysis Program (X-LEAP). The observed magnetospheric SWCX shows an enhanced emission of approximately $I_{\rm OVII}^{\rm mag}\approx 2$ photons $\rm cm^{-2}~ s^{-1}~sr^{-1}$ toward the Sun, showing a consistent shape predicted by numerical simulations. Furthermore, this magnetospheric SWCX exhibits a dependence on the XMM pointing direction, which traces the path length of SWCX emission in the Earth's magnetosphere. Building on this directional dependence, we model the 3D magnetosheath structure using soft X-ray observations for the first time, constraining the averaged boundary geometry and SWCX emissivity distribution over 22 years. Finally, utilizing the XMM data, we derive an empirical O VII emission efficiency of $α_{\rm OVII}=(2.1\pm0.4) \times 10^{-16}\ {\rm eV\,cm^{2}}$.

AI.tldr: This study maps magnetospheric solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) X-ray emission using 22 years of XMM-Newton O VII line data, revealing enhanced emission toward the Sun consistent with simulations, directional dependence tracing magnetospheric path length, and enabling the first 3D magnetosheath modeling from soft X-ray observations.
AI.motivation: The magnetosphere's structure remains observationally uncertain despite its crucial role in protecting Earth from solar activity; this work aims to better constrain magnetospheric geometry using X-ray emission from solar wind charge exchange.
AI.method: The authors extract magnetospheric SWCX in O VII line emission from XMM-Newton data (X-LEAP program) over 22 years, analyze directional dependence relative to XMM pointing, model the 3D magnetosheath structure, and derive empirical O VII emission efficiency.
AI.result: Observed magnetospheric SWCX shows enhanced emission (~2 photons cm⁻² s⁻¹ sr⁻¹) toward the Sun, consistent with simulations; exhibits directional dependence tracing magnetospheric path length; enables first 3D magnetosheath modeling from soft X-rays; yields empirical O VII emission efficiency α_OVII = (2.1±0.4)×10⁻¹⁶ eV·cm².
AI.conclusion: Soft X-ray observations can effectively constrain 3D magnetosheath geometry and SWCX emissivity distribution, providing a novel observational window into magnetospheric structure.

title: The Next Generation Virgo Cluster Survey (NGVS). II. A Catalog of Galaxies in the Virgo Cluster
comment: The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, accepted
summary: The Next Generation Virgo Cluster Survey (NGVS) is a deep, high resolution imaging campaign that used the 1 deg$^2$ MegaCam instrument on the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope to carry out a comprehensive optical survey of the Virgo cluster, from its core to its virial radius. The NGVS covers a contiguous area of 104 deg$^2$ (8.63 Mpc$^2$ at the 16.5 Mpc distance of Virgo) in the $u^*$-,$g$-,$i$-, and $z$-band, with additional limited coverage in $r$. In this paper, we present the final catalog of Virgo galaxies across the entire NGVS area. The catalog includes 3680 galaxies considered to be $bona~fide$ members of the cluster, spanning a factor of 2.5 million in luminosity, from $g = 8.42$ mag to $g = 24.41$ mag ($M_g = -22.67$ mag to $M_g = -6.68$ mag). With 2100 previously uncataloged galaxies, the NGVS catalog augments the number of known Virgo members by a factor 2.3. The catalog is complete down to $g = 18.6$ mag ($M_g=-12.5$ mag, corresponding to a stellar mass $M_* \sim 1.6\times10^7~M_{\odot}$ for an old stellar population) and 50% complete at $g = 22.0$ mag ($M_g=-9.1$ mag, $M_* \sim 6.2\times10^5~M_{\odot}$), three magnitudes deeper than the venerable Virgo Cluster Catalog (VCC), which for over 40 years has served as the reference standard for Virgo. Photometric and structural parameters are derived for all NGVS galaxies and presented in a series of tables, alongside nuclear and morphological classification, as well as stellar masses and, when available, radial velocities.

AI.tldr: The NGVS presents a deep, multi-band optical survey of the Virgo cluster covering 104 deg², producing a final catalog of 3,680 bona fide cluster members. The catalog spans 2.5 million in luminosity (g = 8.42–24.41 mag), includes 2,100 previously uncataloged galaxies (increasing known members by 2.3×), and is complete to g = 18.6 mag (M_g = -12.5 mag) with 50% completeness at g = 22.0 mag (M_g = -9.1 mag) — three magnitudes deeper than the Virgo Cluster Catalog. Photometric, structural, nuclear, morphological, stellar mass, and radial velocity data are provided.
AI.motivation: To provide a deep, homogeneous, and comprehensive optical census of Virgo cluster galaxies (from core to virial radius) that is significantly deeper and more complete than the existing 40-year-old Virgo Cluster Catalog (VCC).
AI.method: The survey used the 1 deg² MegaCam instrument on CFHT to image 104 deg² in u*-, g-, i-, and z-bands (with limited r-band). Photometric and structural parameters were derived for all galaxies; nuclear/morphological classification, stellar masses, and radial velocities were also cataloged.
AI.result: Catalog of 3,680 bona fide Virgo members, spanning g = 8.42–24.41 mag. 2,100 previously uncataloged galaxies increase known members by factor 2.3. Complete to g = 18.6 mag (M_g = -12.5 mag; M_* ~ 1.6×10⁷ M⊙) and 50% complete at g = 22.0 mag (M_g = -9.1 mag; M_* ~ 6.2×10⁵ M⊙) — three magnitudes deeper than VCC.
AI.conclusion: The NGVS delivers the deepest and most complete optical catalog of Virgo cluster galaxies to date, substantially surpassing the VCC in depth and member count, and provides rich multi-parameter data for future studies of cluster galaxy evolution.

title: Semi-Analytical Model for the Evolution of Stellar Binaries in the Empty Loss Cone of Massive Black Holes
summary: Binary star systems orbiting close to a supermassive black hole (SMBH) evolve through encounters with other stars, the SMBH's tidal forces, and the binary's internal dynamics, including general relativistic precession and tides. Many are driven onto highly eccentric inner binary orbits, potentially leading to stellar mergers; other possible outcomes include hypervelocity star ejections or tidal disruption events. We study the evolution of binaries in the empty loss cone regime, where the outer orbit's angular momentum change per orbit due to scattering off other stars is smaller than the outer angular momentum at the tidal separation radius. We build on the work of Hamers \& Samsing to develop a computationally efficient semi-analytical model that captures the long term evolution of binaries in perturbative regimes where the ratio of the binary tidal separation radius to the pericenter around the SMBH is smaller than 0.15. Crucially, we apply corrections to preserve the orthogonality between the binary's eccentricity and angular momentum vectors, which prevents unphysical eccentricity growth. From these simulations, we find analytical fits for the probability distributions of the final orbital parameters of binaries approaching the SMBH. We find that general relativistic precession efficiently suppresses von-Zeipel-Lidov-Kozai-like eccentricity oscillations and reduces the fraction of merging binaries from $84\%$ with Newtonian physics only, to $3\%$ with precession included. Stellar tides further reduce the merger fraction to $0.4\%$.

AI.tldr: This paper studies binary star systems near supermassive black holes in the empty loss cone regime, developing a semi-analytical model with orthogonalization corrections to track long-term evolution. Results show general relativistic precession dramatically reduces merger fractions from 84% to 3%, and stellar tides further suppress it to 0.4%.
AI.motivation: To understand the evolution and final fates of binary star systems orbiting close to supermassive black holes, particularly in the empty loss cone regime where angular momentum changes per orbit are small. Key outcomes of interest include stellar mergers, hypervelocity star ejections, and tidal disruption events.
AI.method: The authors develop a computationally efficient semi-analytical model building on Hamers & Samsing's work, applicable when the ratio of binary tidal separation radius to pericenter around the SMBH is < 0.15. They apply corrections to preserve orthogonality between binary eccentricity and angular momentum vectors to avoid unphysical eccentricity growth, and derive analytical fits for final orbital parameter probability distributions.
AI.result: General relativistic precession efficiently suppresses von-Zeipel-Lidov-Kozai-like eccentricity oscillations. The binary merger fraction decreases from 84% under Newtonian physics alone to 3% with precession included, and further to 0.4% when stellar tides are also considered.
AI.conclusion: Relativistic effects and stellar tides are dominant mechanisms that prevent binary mergers near SMBHs, drastically reducing merger rates compared to Newtonian predictions. The empty loss cone regime yields distinct evolutionary outcomes.

title: Vz-GAL Dusty Star-Forming Galaxies: Revisiting the CO-H2 Conversion Factor Tension
summary: The CO luminosity-to-H$_2$ mass conversion factor ($α_{CO}$) remains a debated uncertainty in determining molecular gas masses of high-redshift dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs). Dynamical mass constraints have often favored $α_{CO}=0.8$~$M_{\odot}~{(K~km~{s}^{-1}~{pc}^{2})}^{-1}$, whereas dust- and radiative-transfer-based methods imply higher values. We revisit this ``tension" using the largest homogeneous sample of 21 unlensed $z\sim1-4$ DSFGs, with securely measured \coonezero luminosities from the VLA \vzgal survey and resolved ($\sim{0.1}^{\prime\prime}$) ALMA 1~mm dust continuum imaging. For 12 galaxies with robust modeling constraints, we derive molecular gas masses using dust spectral energy distribution modeling and the TUNER LVG framework, adopting a solar-metallicity gas-to-dust mass ratio of 100. Although not fully independent due to shared assumptions on dust properties, these approaches yield mutually consistent gas masses corresponding to $α_{CO}\sim1.5-11.5$, with a median near the Galactic $α_{CO}=4.3$. Isotropic virial dynamical masses agree with these gas masses when realistic molecular gas sizes are adopted, while our proposed ``mixed" (rotating, pressure-supported, thick-disk) estimator systematically underestimates dynamical masses, producing low $α_{CO}$ limits. Using GN20 ($z=4.055$) as a case study, we show that resolved gas geometry and kinematics reconcile the discrepancy with LVG-derived $α_{CO}$. Our results suggest that current data do not require $α_{CO}=0.8$, and intermediate to near-Galactic values remain dynamically viable given uncertainties in gas geometry, dust properties, and gas-to-dust ratios. Further progress in calibrating $α_{CO}$ in the early universe will require resolved molecular gas observations, physically motivated ISM modeling, and stringent constraints on dust properties.

AI.tldr: The paper re-evaluates the CO-to-H₂ conversion factor (αCO) in high-redshift dusty star-forming galaxies using a homogeneous sample of 21 unlensed DSFGs from the VLA VzGal survey and ALMA imaging. Results show αCO values range from 1.5–11.5 (median ~4.3, near Galactic), contradicting the commonly assumed αCO=0.8. Dynamical masses agree with gas masses when using realistic molecular gas sizes, and a case study of GN20 demonstrates that resolved gas geometry resolves the apparent tension.
AI.motivation: The CO luminosity-to-H₂ mass conversion factor (αCO) is a key uncertainty in measuring molecular gas masses of high-redshift dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs), with previous studies showing tension between dynamical mass constraints favoring αCO=0.8 and dust/radiative-transfer methods implying higher values.
AI.method: Used a homogeneous sample of 21 unlensed z~1-4 DSFGs with VLA CO(1-0) luminosities and resolved ALMA 1mm dust continuum imaging. For 12 galaxies, derived gas masses via dust SED modeling and the TUNER LVG framework, assuming solar-metallicity gas-to-dust ratio of 100. Compared these to isotropic virial and "mixed" (rotating, pressure-supported, thick-disk) dynamical mass estimators.
AI.result: αCO values range from 1.5–11.5 with a median near Galactic αCO=4.3. Isotropic virial dynamical masses agree with dust/LVG-derived gas masses when realistic molecular gas sizes are used, while the "mixed" estimator systematically underestimates dynamical masses. The GN20 case study shows resolved gas geometry reconciles the discrepancy with LVG-derived αCO.
AI.conclusion: Current data do not require αCO=0.8; intermediate to near-Galactic values remain dynamically viable. Further progress requires resolved molecular gas observations, physically motivated ISM modeling, and stringent dust property constraints.

title: Searching for $γ$-ray emission from a bona fide Compact Symmetric Object sample: a $γ$-ray signal near GB6 J0906+4124
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables; Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: As a particular subclass of active galactic nuclei (AGNs), compact symmetric objects (CSOs) have attracted significant attention due to potential role as young AGNs. Several $γ$-ray emitting CSOs have been detected with Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT), which motivates further searches for more $γ$-ray emitting CSOs. We perform a systematic search for $γ$-ray emission from a bona fide CSO sample using 16 yr Fermi-LAT observation data. No significant $γ$-ray signal is found to be firmly associated with any CSO. Only one $γ$-ray signal is detected near CSO GB6 J0906+4124 with TS = 28.7 ($\sim4.9σ$) in 0.1--300 GeV band. Within the 68\% containment radius of Fermi-LAT average PSF at 3 GeV, GB6 J0906+4124 remains the plausible counterpart of the $γ$-ray signal, primarily due to its classification and broad spectral coverage. This work suggests that GeV emission from CSOs may either be uncommon or simply below the current Fermi-LAT detection sensitivity. Further multi-wavelength follow-up is needed to determine the origin of the $γ$-ray signal near GB6 J0906+4124.

AI.tldr: A systematic search for γ-ray emission from a bona fide CSO sample using 16 years of Fermi-LAT data found no significant association. Only one marginal signal (4.9σ) was detected near GB6 J0906+4124, but GeV emission from CSOs appears either uncommon or below current sensitivity.
AI.motivation: CSOs are considered potential young AGNs, and previous detections of γ-ray emitting CSOs with Fermi-LAT motivated further systematic searches to better understand their high-energy emission properties.
AI.method: Analyzed 16 years of Fermi-LAT observation data to perform a systematic search for γ-ray emission from a bona fide CSO sample.
AI.result: No significant γ-ray signal was firmly associated with any CSO. One signal (TS=28.7, ~4.9σ) was detected near CSO GB6 J0906+4124 in the 0.1–300 GeV band, with GB6 J0906+4124 remaining the plausible counterpart within the 68% containment radius of the Fermi-LAT PSF at 3 GeV.
AI.conclusion: GeV emission from CSOs is likely uncommon or below current Fermi-LAT sensitivity; multi-wavelength follow-up of the GB6 J0906+4124 signal is needed.

title: Morphology-spin connection in the SAMI Galaxy Survey
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: The spin parameter $λ_{\rm{R_e}}$ is a proxy for the specific stellar angular momentum of galaxies and is a useful metric for classifying kinematic morphology. This study aims to quantify the relative importance of galaxy properties in explaining $λ_{\rm{R_e}}$, using data from the Sydney-AAO Multi-object Integral-field spectrograph (SAMI) Galaxy Survey. We apply partial correlation analysis and partial least squares regression to assess the relative contributions of different parameters in explaining $λ_{\rm{R_e}}$. We find that morphology indicators, bulge-to-total ratio within one effective radius ($B/T_\rm{e}$) and ellipticity ($\varepsilon_\rm{e}$), show the strongest correlations with $λ_{\rm{R_e}}$ and play a leading role in the regression analysis. This result statistically confirms the established fast-rotator sequence, in which fast-rotating early-type galaxies form a continuous structural and kinematic sequence with spiral galaxies, with $λ_{\rm{R_e}}$ decreasing as bulge prominence increases. The light-weighted age and stellar mass also exhibit significant correlations, but their contributions are secondary to the morphology indicators in multivariate analyses. We also examine whether the observed trends in $λ_{\rm{R_e}}$ can be reproduced using galaxy properties alone. The morphology indicators (${B/T_\rm{e}}$, $\varepsilon_\rm{e}$) reproduce the overall distribution of observed $λ_{\rm{R_e}}$ with a scatter of about 0.12, while the inclusion of Age_LW and $M_\star$ provides only modest additional improvement. However, these relations do not reproduce the slow-rotator regime well. Overall, our results show that photometric structural parameters best explain $λ_{\rm{R_e}}$ and suggest that statistical inference of galaxy spin from non-IFS observables may become feasible with improved models and a broader set of parameters.

AI.tldr: This study uses SAMI Galaxy Survey data to analyze the spin parameter λ_Re, finding that morphology indicators (bulge-to-total ratio and ellipticity) are the strongest predictors, statistically confirming the fast-rotator sequence, while photometric structural parameters best explain λ_Re and could enable spin inference from non-IFS observables.
AI.motivation: To quantify the relative importance of galaxy properties in explaining the spin parameter λ_Re, a proxy for specific stellar angular momentum and kinematic morphology classification.
AI.method: Applied partial correlation analysis and partial least squares regression to SAMI Galaxy Survey data, assessing contributions of morphology indicators (B/T_e, ε_e), light-weighted age, and stellar mass to λ_Re.
AI.result: Morphology indicators B/T_e and ε_e show strongest correlations with λ_Re, reproducing its distribution with ~0.12 scatter; light-weighted age and stellar mass have secondary contributions; the slow-rotator regime is not well reproduced.
AI.conclusion: Photometric structural parameters best explain λ_Re, statistically confirming the fast-rotator sequence; statistical inference of galaxy spin from non-IFS observables may become feasible with improved models and broader parameter sets.

title: A Type Ia Supernova Candidate at $z\sim4.3$: A Transient Interloper in the Search for $z\sim14$ Galaxies
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is opening a new window into the distant Universe by discovering galaxies and transients in the early Universe. We investigate a high-redshift transient candidate, beacon_1420-5253_4770. This object was initially identified as a high-redshift galaxy candidate at $z\sim14$. However, the source was not detected in epochs before and after the detection epoch, suggesting that the object is a transient source rather than a persistent galaxy. We classify the source by comparing the colors, magnitudes, light curves, and spectral energy distribution with various spectral templates of transients. Our analysis shows that the observed properties are consistent with a Type Ia supernova at $z\sim4.3$. Strong absorption by Fe-group elements seen in Type Ia supernova spectra can mimic the Lyman break used to detect high-redshift galaxies. At $z \sim 4.3$, corresponding to a cosmic age of only $\sim 1.5$ Gyr, our detection provides a direct probe of the delay time between star formation and supernova explosion. Our estimate of the event rate implies a minimum delay time shorter than 1 Gyr. We also discuss the implications of transient contamination for searches of galaxies in the early Universe.

AI.tldr: JWST identified a transient candidate (beacon_1420-5253_4770) initially thought to be a $z\sim14$ galaxy, but reclassified as a Type Ia supernova at $z\sim4.3$ based on colors, light curves, and SED analysis. Fe-group absorption mimics the Lyman break. Detection suggests a minimum delay time between star formation and supernova explosion shorter than 1 Gyr. Implications for transient contamination in high-redshift galaxy searches are discussed.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether a high-redshift galaxy candidate detected by JWST is actually a transient source, and to classify its nature using multi-wavelength and temporal data.
AI.method: Comparison of colors, magnitudes, light curves, and spectral energy distribution (SED) with spectral templates of known transients.
AI.result: The source is a Type Ia supernova at $z\sim4.3$, not a galaxy at $z\sim14$. Fe-group absorption in SN Ia spectra can mimic the Lyman break. The event rate implies a minimum delay time < 1 Gyr.
AI.conclusion: This detection provides a direct probe of delay time between star formation and supernova explosion at a cosmic age of ~1.5 Gyr, and highlights contamination risks for high-redshift galaxy searches.

title: Examining the stellar-merger origin of the blue main sequence in the open cluster NGC\,3532 with N-body simulations
summary: Extended main-sequence turnoffs, extended main sequences, and split main sequences observed in the colour-magnitude diagrams of young and intermediate-age star clusters are now widely interpreted as the consequence of a distribution of stellar rotation rates among their intermediate-mass (1.5-1.8~M$_\odot$) members. However, the origin of the slowly rotating population that occupies the blue main sequence (bMS) remains uncertain, and stellar mergers have been proposed as one possible pathway. We investigate whether stellar mergers can account for the observed bMS population in the 330-Myr Galactic open cluster NGC 3532. We perform fourteen direct NBODY7 simulations spanning different initial cluster masses, radii, binary fractions, and binary orbital distributions. The simulations are selected to reproduce the present-day properties of NGC 3532 within the observational uncertainties, allowing us to estimate the expected number of merger products among its intermediate-mass main-sequence (MS) members. The cluster hosts $\approx 37\%$ bMS members among its intermediate-mass MS population, which are predominantly slow rotators. Despite this large bMS population, our simulations produce only a handful of MS-MS merger products, due to the cluster's low density and substantial mass loss during its evolution. Stellar mergers are unlikely to be the dominant formation channel for the observed slowly rotating bMS population in NGC 3532 and other disperse open clusters. Our results instead favour angular-momentum loss mechanisms operating before or shortly after the zero-age main sequence, such as pre-main-sequence star-disk interactions or tidal synchronization in low-mass ratio binaries.

AI.tldr: This paper uses N-body simulations to show that stellar mergers cannot explain the slowly rotating blue main sequence (bMS) population in NGC 3532, favoring instead angular-momentum loss mechanisms like star-disk interactions or tidal synchronization.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether stellar mergers can account for the observed slowly rotating blue main sequence (bMS) population in the 330-Myr Galactic open cluster NGC 3532, given that the origin of slow rotators among intermediate-mass stars remains uncertain.
AI.method: Fourteen direct NBODY7 simulations varying initial cluster mass, radius, binary fraction, and binary orbital distributions, selected to match the present-day properties of NGC 3532 within observational uncertainties.
AI.result: NGC 3532 has ~37% bMS members (predominantly slow rotators) among intermediate-mass MS stars, but simulations produce only a handful of MS-MS merger products due to the cluster's low density and substantial mass loss.
AI.conclusion: Stellar mergers are unlikely to be the dominant formation channel for the slowly rotating bMS population in NGC 3532 and other disperse open clusters; angular-momentum loss mechanisms (e.g., pre-main-sequence star-disk interactions or tidal synchronization in low-mass ratio binaries) are favored instead.

title: Be/X-Ray Binaries: Phenomenology, Variability, and Accretion~Dynamics
summary: Be/X-ray binaries constitute the largest and most diverse subgroup of neutron star high-mass X-ray binaries. These systems feature a rapidly rotating Be star surrounded by a circumstellar decretion disk that serves as the primary reservoir of accreted matter onto a strongly magnetized neutron star. While a few Be/X-ray binaries remain persistently active, the majority manifest as hard X-ray transient sources, becoming detectable only during X-ray outbursts. This review synthesizes current understanding of their rich phenomenology across optical and X-ray wavelengths, focusing on variability ocurring over timescales that span from seconds to years.

AI.tldr: Be/X-ray binaries are the largest subgroup of neutron star high-mass X-ray binaries, featuring Be stars with circumstellar disks. Most are transient X-ray sources, and this review covers their multi-wavelength variability across timescales from seconds to years.
AI.motivation: To synthesize current understanding of Be/X-ray binaries, which constitute the largest and most diverse subgroup of neutron star high-mass X-ray binaries, and to characterize their rich phenomenology across optical and X-ray wavelengths.
AI.method: A review synthesizing observational data across optical and X-ray wavelengths, focusing on variability spanning timescales from seconds to years.
AI.result: Be/X-ray binaries exhibit rich phenomenology with most manifesting as hard X-ray transient sources, becoming detectable only during X-ray outbursts, while a few remain persistently active.
AI.conclusion: This review consolidates current knowledge of Be/X-ray binary systems, highlighting their multi-timescale variability and the role of the Be star's circumstellar decretion disk as the primary reservoir of accreted matter.

title: Estimating stellar metallicities from Gaia DR3 XP data using LAMOST DR10
summary: Gaia DR3 provides astrophysical parameters for hundreds of millions of stars, but the metallicities [M/H] from its GSP-Phot module suffer from systematic biases. We estimate stellar metallicities from Gaia DR3 data using the homogeneous spectroscopic iron abundances [Fe/H] of LAMOST DR10 as training labels. We cross-matched LAMOST DR10 with Gaia DR3 and trained a gradient-boosted decision-tree regressor (XGBoost) on 1.20 million AFGK stars using only Gaia-derived inputs and proxies. We validated the estimates on held-out LAMOST stars, GALAH DR4, APOGEE DR17, and 46 open clusters, and applied the model to measure the radial metallicity gradient of the Milky Way disk. On the held-out test set, the model achieves a mean absolute error of 0.052 dex and $R^2=0.94$ with negligible bias, compared with 0.242 dex for GSP-Phot on the same stars. The estimates transfer well to external surveys, with mean absolute errors of 0.066 dex for GALAH and 0.068 dex for APOGEE. For open clusters, the median difference between our estimated [Fe/H] and spectroscopic values is 0.041 dex, smaller than both GSP-Phot (0.248 dex) and a previous APOGEE-trained XGBoost model (0.067 dex). Applied to the Galactic disk, our model recovers a broken thin-disk radial gradient, with inner and outer slopes of $+0.119$ and $-0.058\,\mathrm{dex\,kpc^{-1}}$, respectively, and a break near 5.9 kpc, as well as an open-cluster gradient of $-0.066\,\mathrm{dex\,kpc^{-1}}$; both agree with previous high-resolution spectroscopic studies. Our [Fe/H] estimates are accurate to 0.05-0.07 dex for AFGK stars with $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]\gtrsim-2.5$; below this limit, the predictions should be treated as lower bounds. The catalogue and trained model are publicly available on Zenodo and are suitable for chemical studies of the Milky Way.

AI.tldr: A machine-learning model (XGBoost) trained on LAMOST [Fe/H] labels and Gaia DR3 inputs predicts stellar metallicities with ~0.05–0.07 dex accuracy for AFGK stars, significantly outperforming GSP-Phot, and recovers the Milky Way's broken radial metallicity gradient.
AI.motivation: Gaia DR3's GSP-Phot metallicities suffer from systematic biases, motivating the need for more accurate and unbiased stellar metallicity estimates using Gaia data alone.
AI.method: Cross-matched LAMOST DR10 with Gaia DR3; trained an XGBoost regressor on 1.20 million AFGK stars using only Gaia-derived inputs and proxies; validated on held-out LAMOST stars, GALAH DR4, APOGEE DR17, and 46 open clusters.
AI.result: MAE=0.052 dex, R²=0.94 on held-out test set; MAE=0.066 dex (GALAH) and 0.068 dex (APOGEE); open-cluster median difference 0.041 dex; recovered broken thin-disk gradient (inner +0.119, outer −0.058 dex kpc⁻¹) and open-cluster gradient (−0.066 dex kpc⁻¹).
AI.conclusion: The model provides accurate [Fe/H] estimates for AFGK stars with [Fe/H] ≳ −2.5, suitable for Galactic chemical studies; catalog and model are publicly available.

title: Modes in Transitional Millisecond Pulsars: Evidence of Pulsar Wind-Induced Disk Heating from GRMHD and Radiative Transfer
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to ApJL on June 12th
summary: Transitional millisecond pulsars (tMSPs) alternate between radio and X-ray pulsar states, and can represent the missing link between rotation- and accretion-powered neutron stars. Their disk state switches stochastically between the low and high X-ray modes, both of unknown physical origin and less luminous than low-mass X-ray binaries. To reveal the source of the X-ray emission, we carry out 2D axisymmetric general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamical simulations of the interaction between an accretion disk and tMSP magnetosphere. For the first time, we post-process tMSP simulations with a radiative transfer code that incorporates thermal synchrotron, absorption, and Compton scattering processes. By varying the disk density, hence the inflow rate, we explore two disk regimes: one truncated outside and another inside the light cylinder. In the former, most of the X-ray flux comes from the synchrotron emission powered by the wind heating the disk: this "wind" regime could correspond to the high X-ray mode. The latter is the propeller regime and lacks this heating process. However, the propeller episodically expels the disk, activating the wind heating: a 70%-30% mixture of such propeller and wind regimes reproduces the X-ray spectrum of the low X-ray mode. The excess electromagnetic torque in the propeller regime increases the spin-down rate, averaged over both modes, by a few percent above the disk-free radio pulsar state, in agreement with observations. Overall, the system is more luminous in X-rays when the flow is truncated outside the light cylinder and supports a contribution from wind-induced disk heating in both low and high X-ray modes.

AI.tldr: Using 2D GRMHD simulations with radiative transfer post-processing, the paper identifies two X-ray emission regimes in transitional millisecond pulsars: a "wind" regime (disk truncated outside light cylinder, wind-heated synchrotron emission, likely high X-ray mode) and a "propeller" regime (disk inside light cylinder, episodic ejection activating wind heating, mixture producing low X-ray mode). The propeller torque increases spin-down rate by a few percent, matching observations.
AI.motivation: To uncover the physical origin of the low and high X-ray modes in transitional millisecond pulsars (tMSPs), which alternate stochastically between states, and to understand how these systems bridge rotation-powered and accretion-powered neutron stars.
AI.method: 2D axisymmetric general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamical (GRMHD) simulations of accretion disk-magnetosphere interaction in tMSPs, followed by radiative transfer post-processing incorporating thermal synchrotron, absorption, and Compton scattering, with varying disk density/inflow rate to probe two disk truncation regimes (outside vs. inside the light cylinder).
AI.result: Disk truncated outside light cylinder produces X-rays via wind-heated synchrotron (wind regime, high X-ray mode). Disk truncated inside light cylinder (propeller regime) lacks wind heating but episodically expels material; a 70%-30% mixture of propeller and wind regimes matches the low X-ray mode spectrum. Excess torque in propeller regime raises spin-down rate by a few percent over the radio pulsar state.
AI.conclusion: The system is more X-ray luminous when flow truncation occurs outside the light cylinder; wind-induced disk heating contributes to both low and high X-ray modes.

title: Bright Galaxies at Cosmic Dawn: A Cloud-Scale Star Formation Model Unifying Variable SFE, IMFs, and Stochasticity
summary: To investigate the origins of the high abundance of UV-bright galaxies at z > 10, we present a new semi-analytic model that bridges the gap between small-scale star formation physics and large-scale galaxy evolution by explicitly tracking discrete star-forming clouds within smoothly evolving dark matter potentials. Unlike conventional semi-analytic models, our approach naturally captures the stochasticity of star formation, allowing us to isolate how cloud properties, star formation efficiencies (SFEs), and stellar initial mass functions (IMFs) shape the star-formation burstiness of early galaxies. Clouds are drawn sequentially from a cloud mass distribution, assigned an SFE and IMF depending on cloud mass, metallicity, and redshift, and evolve under the influence of short-timescale stellar feedback. We identify three distinct star formation regimes arising from the interplay between cloud masses, densities, and feedback timescales: a stochastic, feedback-limited regime in low-mass halos with long quiescent phases; a bursty regime regulated by the cloud mass distribution; and a smooth, continuous regime in massive halos. Our fiducial model adopts a dynamic IMF, an SFE linked to cloud properties and the IMF, and massive, moderately dense clouds. Varying assumptions reveals that top-heavy IMFs and enhanced SFEs in massive clouds amplify burstiness, while altering the upper cloud mass or density normalisation is secondary. Among model ingredients, the IMF most strongly impacts the UV luminosity function (LF), while switching to a constant SFE boosts the faint end, and reducing the maximum cloud mass decreases the bright end. These results demonstrate that cloud-scale physics critically shape early galaxy UV luminosity distributions.

AI.tldr: A new semi-analytic model tracking discrete star-forming clouds reveals three star formation regimes (stochastic, bursty, smooth) in early galaxies at z>10, showing that cloud-scale physics—particularly the IMF and SFE—critically shape UV luminosity functions.
AI.motivation: To explain the origins of the unexpectedly high abundance of UV-bright galaxies at z > 10, which conventional galaxy formation models struggle to reproduce.
AI.method: A semi-analytic model that bridges small-scale star formation physics and large-scale galaxy evolution by explicitly tracking discrete star-forming clouds within evolving dark matter potentials, with clouds drawn sequentially from a cloud mass distribution and assigned SFEs and IMFs dependent on cloud mass, metallicity, and redshift.
AI.result: Three regimes identified: stochastic/feedback-limited in low-mass halos, bursty regulated by cloud mass distribution, and smooth/continuous in massive halos. Top-heavy IMFs and enhanced SFEs amplify burstiness; IMF most strongly impacts UV LF, constant SFE boosts faint end, reducing maximum cloud mass decreases bright end.
AI.conclusion: Cloud-scale physics critically shape early galaxy UV luminosity distributions, with the IMF as the dominant driver of UV luminosity function variations.

title: Gravitational-Wave Sky Mapping with Pulsar Timing Arrays: The Full Earth-Pulsar Response and Fundamental Resolution Limits
summary:
Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) are the only means to observe nanohertz gravitational waves (GWs). While current analyses primarily exploit the Earth term, the full detector response encodes additional directional information in the pulsar terms. We develop a GW sky-mapping framework based on the complete Earth--pulsar response and a tensor spherical harmonic decomposition of the GW field. This yields closed-form response functions for an elementary baseline and casts PTA sky reconstruction as a linear inverse problem.
  We show that a PTA behaves as a diffraction-limited GW observatory whose angular sensitivity is governed by the dimensionless parameter $ωL$, where $ω$ is the GW angular frequency and $L$ is the pulsar distance. The detector response exhibits four distinct regimes: an Earth-term dominated regime, a transition regime, a pulsar-term-dominated regime, and an exponential sensitivity cutoff at $l_{cut}\simeqωL$. This cutoff defines the fundamental angular resolution limit of PTA sky maps.
  Using Fisher-information and singular-value analyses, we show that the achievable angular resolution is constrained not only by the intrinsic detector response but also by the finite number of pulsars, their sky distribution, and timing noise. In particular, we find that coherent pulsar-term information can improve full-sky gravitational-wave mapping only for PTAs containing of order $N_{trans}\sim10^{11}$ precisely timed pulsars. This result demonstrates that, although the transition to a pulsar-term-sensitive regime exists mathematically, it is inaccessible for realistic PTAs and therefore provides a quantitative justification for the Earth-term approximation adopted in contemporary observations.
  Finally, we extend the formalism to stochastic GW backgrounds, establishing a unified mathematical framework for PTA sky mapping and anisotropy studies.

AI.tldr: Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) can reconstruct gravitational-wave sky maps using both Earth and pulsar terms, but the pulsar-term regime requires ~10^11 precisely timed pulsars, making it practically inaccessible; thus the Earth-term approximation is justified for current observations.
AI.motivation: To develop a complete GW sky-mapping framework for PTAs that incorporates both Earth and pulsar terms via tensor spherical harmonics, and to determine the practical feasibility and angular resolution limits of pulsar-term-enhanced imaging.
AI.method: Tensor spherical harmonic decomposition of the GW field; closed-form response functions for an Earth-pulsar baseline; Fisher-information and singular-value analyses to quantify angular resolution.
AI.result: PTA angular resolution is limited by ωL (GW frequency × pulsar distance), with four regimes: Earth-term-dominated, transition, pulsar-term-dominated, and exponential sensitivity cutoff at l_cut≃ωL. Coherent pulsar-term information only improves full-sky mapping for N_trans~10^11 pulsars, which is unattainable.
AI.conclusion: The Earth-term approximation is quantitatively justified for realistic PTAs; the pulsar-term-sensitive regime, while mathematically possible, is observationally inaccessible.

title: Molecular gas hidden in plain sight in the early Universe
comment: Accepted for publication as Letter to the Editor in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary:
We report the discovery of an extreme intervening molecular absorber at zabs = 4.1 towards the z = 4.7 quasar SDSS J080023.02+305101.22 revealed through strong H2 absorption that had remained unnoticed in archival data for about two decades. The system, which we analysed with new VLT/X-shooter observations, has a metallicity of about one-fifth the solar value, in line with the moderate dust reddening AV~0.06 mag. More strikingly, it exhibits the highest molecular fraction, fH2 = 2N(H2)/(2N(H2) + N(HI))~=60%, measured at z>0 from direct determinations of both atomic and molecular hydrogen column densities. Notably, this fraction is comparable to the very highest values in the Local Group. The inferred fH2 still represents a conservative lower limit to the local molecular fraction since the H i absorption very likely includes atomic gas unrelated to the actual molecular component, as indicated by the wide (Delta v~500 km/s) multi-component low-ionisation metal profile.
  The detection of such a system at early cosmic times is remarkable given the limited number of quasar spectra probing z>4. It suggests an unexpectedly high incidence of H2, with important implications for the evolution of molecular gas. This high incidence may be driven by high average densities and enhanced turbulence at those redshifts. At the same time, our results also highlight possible observational biases, both in quasar selection and in recognising strong H2 absorption, suggesting that a significant fraction of molecular gas may remain undetected, in particular near the peak of star formation. The present system offers a unique benchmark for developing efficient detection algorithms. Further progress will benefit from colour-independent quasar surveys, while constraining the physical conditions and environments of such extreme absorbers will require observations on future extremely large telescopes.

AI.tldr: Discovery of an extreme molecular absorber at z=4.1 towards a z=4.7 quasar, exhibiting the highest molecular fraction (fH2 ≈ 60%) ever measured at z>0 from direct H2 and HI column density determinations, comparable to the highest values in the Local Group.
AI.motivation: To report the discovery of an extreme intervening molecular absorber at z=4.1 that had remained unnoticed in archival data for ~20 years, and to discuss its implications for the evolution of molecular gas at early cosmic times and observational biases in detecting such systems.
AI.method: Analysis of new VLT/X-shooter observations of the quasar SDSS J080023.02+305101.22, measuring metallicity, dust reddening, and both atomic (HI) and molecular hydrogen (H2) column densities to determine the molecular fraction.
AI.result: The system has ~1/5 solar metallicity, moderate dust reddening AV~0.06 mag, and exhibits the highest molecular fraction fH2 ≈ 60% at z>0 from direct measurements, comparable to Local Group values. This is a conservative lower limit as HI absorption likely includes unrelated atomic gas.
AI.conclusion: The detection suggests an unexpectedly high incidence of H2 at early cosmic times, possibly driven by high densities and turbulence. It highlights observational biases in quasar selection and H2 recognition, implying significant undetected molecular gas near the peak of star formation. Further progress requires colour-independent quasar surveys and future ELT observations.

title: An (in)complete NIRSpec census of Balmer absorption in Type 1 AGN -- radiation-driven outflows in little red dots, quasars and variable stars
comment: 20 pages, 18 figures, submitted to MNRAS, comments welcome
summary: A notable achievement of the first generation of JWST surveys was the discovery of an abundance of faint high-redshift ($z > 4$) broad-line active galactic nuclei (AGN) in the $L_{\rm bol} < 10^{45}$~erg~s$^{-1}$ regime, previously only accessible at $z < 1$. The high prevalence of absorption features in their broad hydrogen lines is one of the peculiarities of a significant fraction of this new population. In this paper, we conduct a broad census of Balmer absorption in a sample of 47 Type-1 AGN spanning $2 < z < 7$. Accounting for incompleteness of JWST spectroscopic data, we estimate that $44_{-6}^{+21}$~\% of Little Red Dots (LRDs) have absorption in \Has while the incidence rate is $< 25$~\% (at 2$σ$) in Little Blue Dots (LBDs). Additionally, R1000 JWST/NIRSpec data is strongly resolution limited, implying an inability to disentangle Doppler broadening in the absorption from optical depth effects. This is alleviated with R2700 observations, although some degeneracies remain. We find a significant correlation between the velocity of the Balmer absorption and the [OIII]5007 narrow line luminosity, suggesting a common driving mechanism. We do not find any other significant correlations (and do not confirm previously claimed correlations) between Balmer absorption and other spectral properties of LRDs (except for the expected correlation between \Has and \Hbs absorption velocities). Comparing LRDs, quasars and stellar \Has absorbers, we establish that absorption in both LRDs and broad absorption line quasars is consistent with radiatively driven outflows, echoing the physics of variable stars yet occurring at vastly different scales.

AI.tldr: JWST reveals 44% of Little Red Dots (high-z AGN) show Balmer absorption, driven by radiatively driven outflows, while incidence is <25% in Little Blue Dots. Absorption velocity correlates with [OIII] luminosity, suggesting a common driving mechanism.
AI.motivation: To characterize the peculiar Balmer absorption features discovered in faint high-redshift broad-line AGN from JWST surveys, which were previously inaccessible at z<1, and understand its physical origin and incidence across AGN subpopulations (LRDs vs. LBDs).
AI.method: Census of Balmer absorption in 47 Type-1 AGN at 2<z<7 using JWST/NIRSpec (R1000 and R2700), accounting for spectroscopic incompleteness, with correlation analysis against [OIII] luminosity and other spectral properties.
AI.result: ~44% of LRDs show Hα absorption vs. <25% in LBDs; R1000 data is resolution-limited (cannot separate Doppler broadening from optical depth); significant correlation between Balmer absorption velocity and [OIII] luminosity; no other correlations confirmed.
AI.conclusion: Balmer absorption in LRDs and broad absorption line quasars is consistent with radiatively driven outflows, analogous to variable star physics but at vastly different scales.

title: Physical Properties of 6.7 Million Galaxies from the DESI Bright Galaxy Survey: Spectral Fitting and Systematic Tests with Mock Spectra
summary: We present a comprehensive analysis of the physical properties of galaxies in the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Data Release 1 (DR1) Bright Galaxy Survey (BGS), based on full spectral fitting of $\sim 6.7$ million galaxy spectra. Using a customized spectral fitting pipeline, we derive key physical parameters including stellar mass, stellar velocity dispersion, stellar population age, dust attenuation, and emission-line properties. To quantify the reliability and systematic uncertainties of our measurements, we construct a large set of mock spectra that closely reproduce the observed properties of DESI data, including realistic noise and spectral features. By comparing the recovered parameters with the known inputs, we assess the performance of the spectral fitting as a function of stellar continuum signal-to-noise ratio (S/N, defined as the ratio of the median continuum flux to its associated error) and redshift. We find that stellar masses can be robustly recovered with negligible bias for spectra with $\mathrm{S/N} \gtrsim 5$, while low-S/N spectra ($\mathrm{S/N} \lesssim 5$) show a mild systematic overestimation of $\sim 0.1$ dex and increased scatter. Similar trends are observed for stellar population parameters, while emission-line fluxes are recovered with high accuracy and minimal bias. We further validate our stellar mass estimates by comparison with independent measurements from photometric spectral energy distribution fitting, finding good overall consistency within the expected systematic uncertainties. The value-added catalog presented in this work enables a wide range of statistical studies of galaxy evolution with DESI, and provides a foundation for future analyses.

AI.tldr: DESI DR1 BGS provides robust physical galaxy parameters from ~6.7 million spectra via full spectral fitting, validated with mock spectra, showing reliable stellar mass recovery at S/N≳5 with systematic biases quantified for low-S/N data.
AI.motivation: To enable statistical studies of galaxy evolution by deriving and validating key physical properties (stellar mass, velocity dispersion, age, dust attenuation, emission lines) from the large DESI DR1 Bright Galaxy Survey dataset.
AI.method: Customized full spectral fitting pipeline applied to ~6.7 million DESI BGS spectra; reliability assessed using mock spectra with realistic noise and spectral features, comparing recovered vs. input parameters as function of S/N and redshift; validated against independent photometric SED fitting.
AI.result: Stellar masses recovered with negligible bias at S/N≳5; mild systematic overestimation (~0.1 dex) and increased scatter for S/N≲5; emission-line fluxes recovered with high accuracy and minimal bias; good consistency with photometric SED fitting results.
AI.conclusion: The value-added catalog provides a robust foundation for statistical galaxy evolution studies with DESI, with quantified systematic uncertainties for different S/N regimes.

title: The Large Magellanic Cloud through the lens of the James Webb Space Telescope: Binaries and the mass function in the galaxy's outskirts
comment: 10 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Nearby galaxies such as the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) offer an ideal laboratory to test the initial mass function under different physical conditions, but previous works have been limited by photometric depth and have therefore poorly constrained the low-mass regime. Here, we analyze ultra-deep James Webb Space Telescope observations of a field in the LMC outskirts, near the intermediate-age and massive star cluster NGC 1846. Using the $m_{\rm F322W2}$ versus $m_{\rm F115W}-m_{\rm F322W2}$ color-magnitude diagram, we derive the mass function (MF) down to unprecedentedly low masses ($M=0.17 M_{\odot}$), explicitly accounting for the contribution of unresolved binaries, whose fraction is constrained directly from the data. For systems with mass ratios $q>0.6$, we measure a binary fraction of $f_{\rm bin}^{q>0.6}=0.15\pm0.01$, implying a total binary fraction of $f_{\rm bin}^{\rm TOT}=0.34\pm0.02$ for a flat mass-ratio distribution. This is consistent with values in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) and in the Milky Way field, suggesting similar binary formation efficiency across low-density environments. We also derive the MF over the mass interval 0.17-0.82 $M_{\odot}$ and fit it with a power law, obtaining a slope of $α= -1.49 \pm 0.16$. This slope is shallower than the canonical Salpeter value ($α=-2.35$) and slightly shallower than that measured in the SMC field, while remaining consistent with determinations for Galactic open clusters and for several clusters in the Magellanic Clouds and the Milky Way. Together, these results support a scenario in which both binary formation efficiency and the shape of the low-mass MF depend only weakly on the environment.

AI.tldr: Using ultra-deep JWST observations of the LMC outskirts near NGC 1846, the authors derive the mass function down to 0.17 M☉, measure a binary fraction of ~34%, and find a power-law MF slope of α=−1.49±0.16 — shallower than Salpeter and consistent with a weak environmental dependence on both binary formation and low-mass MF shape.
AI.motivation: To test the initial mass function under different physical conditions using nearby galaxies as laboratories, particularly constraining the poorly explored low-mass regime with deeper photometric data.
AI.method: Ultra-deep JWST observations (F115W, F322W2) of an LMC field near NGC 1846; analysis using color-magnitude diagrams; binary fraction constrained directly from data; MF derived over 0.17–0.82 M☉ and fitted with a power law.
AI.result: Binary fraction of 0.34±0.02 (total) and 0.15±0.01 for q>0.6; power-law MF slope α=−1.49±0.16, shallower than Salpeter (−2.35) and slightly shallower than SMC field but consistent with Galactic open clusters and other Magellanic Cloud clusters.
AI.conclusion: Both binary formation efficiency and the shape of the low-mass IMF depend only weakly on the environment.
